video_title: Bond Vigilantes: Fed Needs To Get Ahead Of Inflation
gist: In a chart-driven weekly briefing (recorded July 27), Ed Yardeni argues the S&P 500 is in a 'summer stall' near 7,500 while the 2-year Treasury at 4.33% is demanding the Fed reverse its three 2025 rate cuts, and he now expects a quarter-point HIKE as soon as Wednesday under Fed chair Kevin Warsh. He also flags that Alphabet's SpaceX-related mark-to-market gain distorted Q2 S&P 500 earnings growth (35% reported vs 23% underlying), keeps an 8,250 year-end S&P target on ~$410 forward earnings times a 20-21 PE, and straddles the semiconductor debate between extreme cyclicality (51% margins, 62.7% long-term growth expectations) and a structural AI boom.

insights.claim: The S&P 500 has been hovering around 7,500 since May 14 after bottoming on March 30, and Yardeni expects the range to persist rather than break either way — what he earlier called a 'June swoon' has turned into a 'summer stall'.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Argues for range-trading / premium-selling and against chasing breakouts in the index until the Fed and AI-capex questions resolve.
insights.quote: I don't think we're going to see a a big plunge in the market here. I don't think we're going to go up a lot.

insights.claim: The March 2026 selloff driven by the Middle East war proved to be a pullback rather than a correction or bear market, which Yardeni treats as fresh confirmation of his framework that geopolitical crises are buying opportunities.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Sets a playbook for the next Hormuz/Red Sea headline shock: buy the geopolitical dip rather than de-risk.
insights.quote: consistent with the notion that uh the geopolitical crises have in the past been buying opportunities and so far that seems to apply to what happened in in March

insights.claim: Yardeni reads the market's internal rotation — transports, railroads, small caps, financials and industrials outperforming while AI-levered software and semis get hit — as healthy broadening that keeps the bull market intact, and Yardeni Research has published a 'US sectors call' quick takes with six overweights and consumer discretionary/consumer durables as underweight candidates.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Favors barbelling out of crowded AI winners into cyclical value pockets while staying long the index.
insights.quote: let's just go to transportation stocks. Let's go to railroads. Uh let's go to financials. Let's go to industrials.

themes.theme: Warsh Fed leaning toward a hike

insights.claim: Fed chair Kevin Warsh has publicly planted himself on the price-stability side, noting inflation has run above 2% for more than five years and signalling it is time to force it back to target — a hawkish reaction function markets have not fully priced.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A Fed chair anchored on a five-year inflation overshoot means the policy distribution is skewed to hikes, not cuts — bearish front-end duration.

insights.claim: Yardeni had abandoned his call for a July Fed rate hike after the CPI and PPI reports but has reinstated it, now viewing a quarter-point hike at Wednesday's FOMC as very likely, while the market still assigns the highest odds to September.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A hike this week versus September is a live mispricing in fed funds futures and short-end rates.

insights.claim: Yardeni predicts an asymmetric dissent pattern at this FOMC: if the Fed stands pat there will be dissenters demanding a hike, but if it hikes there will be no dissents, because the on-hold camp does not feel strongly enough to formally dissent.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Dissents on a hold would be read as a pre-commitment to September, so the statement's dissent line is the tradable detail even if rates are unchanged.
insights.quote: if they if they do nothing, there'll be dissenters and if they actually raise rates, I don't think there'll be any dissenters

themes.theme: 2-year Treasury as the Fed's marching orders

insights.claim: With the 2-year Treasury yield at 4.33%, the bond market is effectively telling the Fed to reverse all three of last year's rate cuts (75 basis points total) with three hikes over the next two years; Yardeni's own read is that at least one of those cuts should be reversed sooner rather than later.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete level to watch: as long as the 2-year holds above the funds rate, the front end stays a short and rate-cut trades stay wrong-footed.
insights.quote: I would say that the 2-years right now is saying reverse at least one of those and do it sooner rather than later.

insights.claim: Warsh's stated doctrine is to give less Fed forward guidance and take more guidance from markets, on the logic that not polluting the bond market with officials' views yields a cleaner market signal of what policy should be — making the 2-year yield the operative policy input, which Yardeni endorses.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: If the Fed follows the 2-year instead of leading it, rate expectations become self-reinforcing and Fedspeak loses information value relative to the curve.
insights.quote: say less, watch the market

insights.claim: Yardeni's chart of the 2-year yield minus the official policy rate of each major central bank shows every case pointing the same direction — not easing, not even holding, but tightening.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A globally synchronized hawkish signal argues against long-duration sovereign bonds and against rate-cut-dependent trades outside the US too.
insights.quote: the 2-year in all these circumstances is saying uh definitely uh don't think about easing. Uh don't even think about uh holding. Uh think about uh tightening.

themes.theme: Oil's round trip above and below $90

insights.claim: Crude round-tripped from roughly $100 a barrel to below $90 within days as the on-again, off-again Middle East war paused, but because the drop came at the very end of July it will not spare the July inflation data, which still carries an energy shock from the earlier spike plus higher gasoline and diesel spot prices.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Sets up a hot July CPI print even though spot energy has already deflated — a fade opportunity if markets extrapolate that print forward.

insights.claim: Yardeni finds it extraordinary how quickly oil fell despite unresolved Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea disruptions, concluding that the pre-war oil bear market conditions — ample supply and flat Chinese demand — are still in force beneath the geopolitical premium.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Implies geopolitical oil spikes are sellable rather than the start of a sustained energy bull market; bearish energy equities' premium.
insights.quote: it is really quite extraordinary at the extent to which despite uh the Strait of Hormuz situation and the uh Red Sea situation that how how quickly and easily oil prices can come down

insights.claim: Chinese oil imports dropped hugely in June, and Yardeni frames the open question as whether China physically could not get barrels or simply refused to pay the elevated price — with strategic reserve drawdowns in China, the US SPR and likely Europe cushioning the low-inventory bull case.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: If China was price-rationing rather than supply-constrained, Chinese restocking becomes a bid under oil at lower prices and a cap above.

insights.claim: Stripping out the friendlier components of the CPI and PPI still leaves super-core inflation — services excluding energy and excluding housing — running on the hot side, which is the core of the case for the Fed to tighten.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Super-core is the print investors should watch to judge whether the hiking case survives the oil rollover.

insights.claim: AI demand has become a direct source of consumer goods inflation: import price indexes for computers, accessories and electronic components including semiconductors have all risen, and Yardeni expects July data to show Apple raising prices.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A novel inflation channel — AI hardware scarcity feeding CPI goods — that keeps the Fed hawkish and squeezes device-maker margins or consumer wallets.
insights.quote: Meanwhile, we also have inflation coming from AI.

insights.claim: The New York Fed's global supply chain pressure index correlates well with goods CPI and Yardeni believes Middle East disruption is still elevating it, because commodities other than oil also transit the strait and can push prices up.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
entities: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
insights.so_what: Goods inflation can stay sticky even with oil back below $90 — watch the supply chain pressure index as a leading indicator for goods CPI.

insights.claim: Tariffs are back after the administration switched to a different authorization statute to justify them, adding a fresh goods-side inflation impulse.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Reinstated tariffs under a new legal basis mean import-cost inflation is a policy constant, not a resolved risk, for goods retailers and their margins.
insights.quote: Tariffs looks like tariffs are back the administration's tried a different authorization statute for justifying tariffs so they're back

insights.claim: The reason Yardeni views the current inflation episode as less troublesome than the earlier post-pandemic one is the absence of a wage-price spiral — while conceding inflation is still nowhere near 2%.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Wage data is the tripwire: a spiral would convert a one-or-two-hike error correction into a genuine tightening cycle and break the equity range.
insights.quote: perhaps why why this one isn't as troublesome is we've yet to see a wage price spiral

themes.theme: GDP optics vs real final demand

insights.claim: The Atlanta Fed's Q2 real GDP estimate was cut from 1.7% to 1.6%, but Yardeni attributes most of that weakness to the AI boom itself — surging imports of semiconductor and memory chips from South Korea and Taiwan subtract from a production-based GDP measure even as US final demand and private investment stay strong.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Soft headline GDP driven by AI imports is not a slowdown signal and should not be traded as a reason for Fed cuts.
insights.quote: most of that weakness was because of the AI boom. We don't make a lot of everything that we need for the AI boom.

insights.claim: The New York Fed's weekly economic index, which has tracked year-over-year real GDP growth well recently, is consistent with roughly 2.7-2.9% real growth, and rail car loadings are also improving — possibly carrying materials and equipment bound for data centers.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
entities: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
insights.so_what: High-frequency trackers running near 3% support the no-recession, hawkish-Fed combination and the industrial/rail rotation trade.

insights.claim: The labor market is tight but decelerating at the margin: initial claims fell sharply with no layoffs, while ADP employment gains are slowing again after a spring rebound from weather-depressed January-February, and Indeed job postings have leveled off with openings still high but well below pandemic peaks.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A labor market that is cooling on supply rather than cracking on demand removes the Fed's excuse to cut and keeps the hike case alive.

insights.claim: Yardeni suspects part of the slowdown in hiring is a supply problem — a skills mismatch — rather than weak labor demand, and he flags payback effects in consumer data with retail sales growth slowing to a still-solid 8% now that the World Cup and tax refunds are behind.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Distinguishes a genuine consumer rollover from calendar payback — 8% retail sales growth argues consumer discretionary weakness is timing, not trend, but Yardeni still leans underweight there.

insights.claim: Alphabet's Q2 report contained a huge capital gain — Yardeni and Joe Abbott attribute a good part of it to Alphabet's large SpaceX stake — that lifted reported S&P 500 Q2 earnings growth to about 35% versus the roughly 23% analysts expected; excluding the gain, growth is right at the expected 23%.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: The headline earnings beat is an accounting artifact — investors extrapolating 35% growth are overpaying for a non-recurring mark-to-market gain.
insights.quote: Alphabet reported last last week a huge capital gain and a good part of that was probably uh SpaceX

insights.claim: Because forward earnings are a time-weighted blend of 2026 and 2027 estimates, the Alphabet other-income gain has polluted the 2026 number, but 2027 is a clean number since analysts are almost certainly not plugging in mark-to-market gains — so 2027 is the estimate that matters from here.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Shifting the analytical anchor to 2027 estimates filters out the distortion and is where the real earnings momentum signal lives.
insights.quote: I doubt that the analysts are plugging anything for other income gains um mark-to-market gains in 2027. So I think this is actually a clean number

insights.claim: Yardeni's PE-times-E arithmetic gets him to an 8,250 year-end S&P 500 target: forward earnings that consensus put a little over $400 per share now look like they are heading to $410, and a 20 to 21 forward multiple on that gets there (a 20 multiple alone gives 8,000).
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A concrete, decomposable index target — roughly 10% above the 7,500 stall — with the two inputs an investor can independently track.
insights.quote: we're big fans of PE times E, I mean that's the it's the arithmetic of the market

insights.claim: The apparent decline in the S&P 500's forward PE is exaggerated because the E is inflated by the mark-to-market gain, whereas the undistorted Buffett ratio remains very high — so the market is not cheap.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Kills the 'multiples are de-rating, so stocks got cheap' argument; valuation offers no cushion if earnings momentum stalls.
insights.quote: you're not going to get that kind of distortion in the Buffett ratio. And that's obviously still very very high. So market is market isn't cheap.

themes.theme: AI capex ROI and the semiconductor cycle

insights.claim: Alphabet posted cloud earnings up roughly 82% with a backlog above $500 billion, yet the stock reaction was dominated by free cash flow turning negative — the same free-cash-flow anxiety that hit Tesla.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Signals that the market's scoring function for hyperscalers has flipped from revenue growth to cash conversion — a re-rating risk for the heaviest AI spenders regardless of demand.

insights.claim: The market's central 'known unknown' is not whether hyperscalers are spending on AI infrastructure but what return they earn on it, with the bear case that companies in an arms race do stupid things and overspend.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Defines the swing variable for the whole AI complex — ROI disclosure, not capex size, is what will re-rate these names.
insights.quote: we know that they're spending a lot of money on AI infrastructure but the known unknown is what kind of return are they going to get on it?

insights.claim: Yardeni sides with the hyperscalers against the overspending bears: the cloud business is already producing the revenue, the hyperscalers probably wish they had more capacity right now because demand exists today, and they are convinced that demand will not suddenly collapse — though he concedes nobody knows for sure and the market clearly has AI fatigue.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Supports staying long the capex chain (cloud, semis, data-center inputs) as long as cloud revenue and backlog growth keep validating the spend.
insights.quote: when you do a are in a a war in an arms race you do stupid things and maybe they shouldn't be spending this kind of money

insights.claim: Semiconductor profit margins are running around 51%, with some components even higher, and Yardeni attributes much of that to prices — which can come back down — making it his flagged 'problem with profit margins' in the group.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Price-driven 51% margins are the most mean-reverting part of the semi earnings story; a pricing rollover would hit estimates even with volumes intact.

insights.claim: Analysts' long-term earnings growth expectations have hit an all-time record 25% per year over the next three to five years for the S&P 500, 41% for information technology and 62.7% for semiconductors — levels Yardeni calls not doable and a mark of irrational exuberance, which also makes the PEG ratio useless as a valuation tool.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Screens that rank stocks as cheap on PEG are being fooled by fantasy growth rates — a source of hidden downside in AI-adjacent 'value'.
insights.quote: all-time record high 25% per year over the next 3 to 5 years. Uh that's not not doable.

insights.claim: Yardeni openly straddles the semiconductor debate — the year-over-year change in semi forward earnings is extremely cyclical and what may lie ahead rhymes with the tech bubble and tech wreck, yet he leans toward semis being a good long-term investment because demand may be structural rather than cyclical, citing Jensen Huang's claim that the world will need 10 times current semiconductor production.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Frames semi drawdowns as buying opportunities within a structural boom, but with the tech-wreck analog as the explicit risk case to monitor.
insights.quote: I'm I'm leaning towards the idea that semiconductors are a good long-term investment.

insights.claim: Software stocks were hit first by AI concerns and semiconductor stocks are now being sold despite very low PEs, which Yardeni explains with the cyclical rule that PEs are typically lowest when earnings are greatest — so cheap-looking semis after massive year-to-date gains are a peak-earnings signal rather than a valuation bargain.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Explains why low-PE semis keep falling and sets the condition for the selloff to end: proof the earnings are structural rather than peak-cycle.
insights.quote: nothing goes straight up as far as I in my experience in the market without coming more often than not straight down

insights.claim: The rising nominal 10-year Treasury yield is being led by the TIPS real yield rather than by inflation expectations, so Yardeni questions whether this is really bond vigilantism at all: breakeven inflation has not risen despite the oil spike and is close to the 10-year 10-year forward inflation-linked swap, implying the yield rise reflects better-than-expected growth.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Growth-led rather than inflation-led yield increases are far more tolerable for equities — watch breakevens, not nominal yields, for the point at which rising rates become an equity problem.
insights.quote: expected inflation really hasn't gone up um despite the oil price and all that
